name: Fortify Health Value of Incubation Grants [June 2019]
summary: Funds Fortify Health's early growth as it helps flour mills in India add iron to wheat flour. GiveWell's spreadsheet "Fortify Health Value of Incubation Grants [June 2019]", linked from its grant page. Every number is traced from the sheet's bottom line; calculated rows reproduce the sheet's own values.

P(Scenario 1): Further intervention level research makes FH look not cost-effective
rows.explainer: I suspect Josh/Stephan will have a better intuition about this parameter, because I was not involved in the intervention level analysis. Josh seemed particularly concerned about adult cognitive benefits, and these comprise 53% of the value of Fortify Health's program, so this seems like a reasonably high risk - which is why I have chosen a 30% value.

rows.label: P(Scenario 2): Further research on applying the academic estimates to FH's program makes FH look not cost-effective.
rows.explainer: There are several outstanding questions regarding the effect size estimate that we use in the CEA. I think that most of these could move us in either direction. However, there are a few downside risks that I am concerned about, which include: 1) we find out that FH consumers' diets contain a lot of tea and we think that is justification for a large reduction in the effect size estimate because tea severely inhibits the absorption of iron from NaFeEDTA, 2) we believe that initial iron status for FH's beneficiaries is so much higher than in the academic studies that they absorb much less iron than we have assumed, 3) the distribution of consumption is highly uneven and in such a way that a large proportion of the product is consumed by people who are no longer receiving benefits from additional iron absorption, 4) a large amount of FH's product is wasted - most likely either because demand

rows.label: P(Scenario 3): Fortify Health have operational problems which means they fail to scale up the program
rows.explainer: They have demonstrated their ability to scale up from nothing to four millers in one year, sound like they have built trust with some useful government officials, and have several potential miller partners who have already expressed interest - so I think this probability is fairly low. The main worry that I have in mind here is that Brendan is going to leave for medical school in August 2019 and I fear that he may have been an important driving force behind their success to date - his leaving may slow things down considerably.

rows.label: P(Scenario 4): Some other unforeseen obstacle prevents us from wanting to recommend them as a top charity
rows.explainer: I guess there are other things that we expect of our top charities - e.g. a very high level of transparency, and it takes quite a lot of engagement with us to reach that status which requires a lot of capacity from the charity's side. It's possible that these could act as barriers. Though their values seem pretty aligned with ours so I'd guess this is a pretty low probability.

Cost of additional grants before top charity status is judged
rows.explainer: We are proposing a $1m grant for the next year, ~half of which is an exit grant. I very strongly doubt we will be ready to judge them for top charity status by July 2020 (as there is a lot more investigation work to be done), so I have assumed that we would need to make one additional year's worth of an incubation grant before making a top charity status decision in July 2021. I suspect that they will make some progress over the next year and so would want a slightly larger grant next year, but they wouldn't require much more in the way of an exit grant, and so I have assumed that next year's grant would be roughly the same size (another $1m) as this year.

rows.label: Probability that we want them to run an RCT/similarly intense level of monitoring because we are too unsure about the benefits
Additional costs in the event that we want them to run an RCT/intense level of monitoring before we judge for top charity status
rows.explainer: This is a very rough estimate, and assumes that we would like to see a pretty high level of M&E - perhaps even an RCT. This would also probably push back our ability to make a decision about top charity status (it would probably take a couple of years before we would get results from an RCT), but I have so far ignored that and still assumed that we would be ready to evaluate by July 2021.

Multiplying by GiveWell's value of a dollar to GiveDirectly converts it into units of value per dollar, so it ranks against the other models.
